title: Jotai 3.0 Ships as a Modernized, ESM-Only Package That Drops Legacy Builds and Deprecated APIs
gist: Jotai's v3.0.0 stable release drops CommonJS/UMD/SystemJS builds entirely to go ESM-only, removes long-deprecated APIs like atomFamily and loadable (migrated to separate packages), and is positioned as a deliberate cleanup rather than reinvention, cementing Jotai as the de facto successor to Facebook's now-deprecated Recoil in the atomic React state management space.

themes.theme: What changed in v3 and why

insights.claim: Jotai v3 drops the CommonJS build entirely, shipping as ES modules only, and also removes UMD and SystemJS bundles, older Node/React/TypeScript support, and the jotai/babel plugin, moving to a module-first structure targeting ES2020 and reading NODE_ENV directly instead of using build-time replacement.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Signals the JS ecosystem's continued consolidation away from CommonJS toward ESM-only distribution — teams still on CJS toolchains or older Node/TypeScript versions must upgrade infrastructure before adopting Jotai v3.
insights.locator: v3 drops the CommonJS build entirely

insights.claim: Maintainer Daishi Kato has long documented the 'dual package hazard' of shipping both CJS and ESM simultaneously, and the ESM-only stance in v3 is presented as the conclusion of that effort, trading broader compatibility for a leaner core with less to maintain.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The 'dual package hazard' rationale is a template other library maintainers can point to when justifying their own eventual ESM-only migrations, suggesting this pattern will spread further across the npm ecosystem.
insights.locator: Maintainer Daishi Kato has long documented the dual package hazard

insights.claim: Despite being marketed as 'no breaking changes,' v3 removes several public APIs including atomFamily, loadable, and the setSelf argument to atom read functions, and redesigns the internal building blocks API — but each removed API had already been deprecated across the late v2 line, so teams that heeded prior deprecation warnings should upgrade cleanly.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The gap between marketing ('no breaking changes') and actual API removals is a recurring pattern in library major-version releases; teams should always audit deprecation warnings before treating a 'compatible' major bump as a no-op upgrade.
insights.quote: a mostly backward-compatible update, dropping some legacy support and deprecated APIs
insights.locator: The releases page echoes that framing

insights.claim: atomFamily now lives in a dedicated jotai-family package with an identical API plus a new atomTree helper, making migration a single import-path swap for most teams; loadable users are migrated to a separate jotai-eager package.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Low-friction migration paths (single import swap) reduce upgrade risk and suggest fast ecosystem-wide adoption of v3 is plausible, unlike migrations requiring substantial rewrites.
insights.locator: atomFamily now lives in the dedicated jotai-family package

insights.claim: Maintainer Daishi Kato confirmed that new features and deeper breaking changes were deliberately kept out of scope for 3.0, with concurrent-safe atoms and external-store syncing deferred to a later v3.x release or a future v4.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Signals more significant Jotai capability changes (concurrent-safe atoms, external-store syncing) are coming in future releases — worth tracking for teams building on React concurrent features or cross-framework state syncing.
insights.locator: Kato confirmed that new features and deeper breaking changes

insights.claim: By making 3.0 a cleanup rather than a reinvention, the Jotai team is betting that a smaller, modern, ESM-native core is the more valuable upgrade for the ecosystem it now anchors.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A conservative, incremental major-version strategy (versus a risky rewrite) reduces ecosystem fragmentation risk and may be a model for other mature open-source libraries balancing modernization against backward compatibility.
insights.locator: By making 3.0 a cleanup rather than a reinvention

themes.theme: Competitive landscape: atomic vs. store-centric state management

insights.claim: Facebook's Recoil, the project that popularized the atomic state model, is now widely treated as deprecated, leaving Jotai as the de facto successor for the atomic model, while its Poimandres sibling Zustand holds the store-centric camp for teams preferring a single external store.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Confirms Jotai's consolidated market position as the leading atomic-state library following Recoil's effective abandonment by Facebook/Meta — a clear signal for React ecosystem tooling investment and adoption decisions.
insights.locator: Facebook's Recoil, the project that popularised atoms, is now widely treated as deprecated

insights.claim: One user in the Ideas for v3 thread pushed back on removing setSelf, describing an optimistic atomWithStorageWhileRevalidate pattern (hydrating from localStorage while fetching fresh server data) that has no clean replacement without it.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A concrete unmet use case (optimistic localStorage hydration pattern) flagged by the community as broken by the v3 API removal — a potential adoption friction point for apps relying on that specific pattern.
insights.locator: In the Ideas for v3 thread, one user pushed back

insights.claim: The same community thread carries a detailed, unresolved request for a first-class default store lifecycle so tests can reset state without reaching into internal APIs, described as a real pain point for large apps relying on getDefaultStore().
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Testing/state-reset ergonomics remain an open gap in Jotai's API surface even after this cleanup release, a signal for what a future minor/major release might need to address.
insights.locator: carries a detailed request for a first-class default store lifecycle
